item.title: Organ Preservation With Watch and Wait in Patients With Rectal Cancer
item.dc:creator: Stephanie S. Keeling
Ramy Behman
Chung-Yuan Hu
John K. Lin
Naveen Manisundaram
Jeongyoon Moon
Brian K. Bednarski
Tsuyoshi Konishi
item.description:
Authors: Stephanie S. Keeling, Ramy Behman, Chung-Yuan Hu, John K. Lin, Naveen Manisundaram, Jeongyoon Moon, Brian K. Bednarski, Tsuyoshi Konishi, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640267
Abstract: Importance With growing evidence and evolving guidelines, organ preservation with watch and wait for stage II to III rectal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy is increasingly implemented. However, the true frequency of watch-and-wait use is unknown. Objective To estimate rates of intentional organ preservation with watch and wait by evaluating secular trends across age groups. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used data from the National Cancer Database (NCDB), with analyses conducted in September 2025. Patients with stage II to III rectal cancer diagnosed between 2006 and 2023 who received neoadjuvant chemoradiation in Commission on Cancer–accredited hospitals participating in the NCDB across the US were included. Exposure Age, year of diagnosis, and treatment strategy (proctectomy vs nonsurgical management). Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome consisted of watch-and-wait rates, defined as excess nonsurgical management greater than baseline. To account for nonsurgical management unrelated to the decision for watch and wait, joinpoint regression estimated baseline rates of nonsurgical management and annual percentage changes. A secondary analysis examined associations of age and year with watch-and-wait rates using multivariable logistic regression. Results Among 101 001 patients with rectal cancer (median [IQR] age, 60 [51-69] years; 37 957 female [37.58%]), 84 324 underwent surgery and 16 677 did not. Baseline rates of nonsurgical management remained stable through 2014. Joinpoints occurred in 2014 and 2019, with annual percentage changes of −0.45% (95% CI, −2.26% to 0.78%; P = .42) in 2006 to 2014, 9.83% (95% CI, 4.66% to 13.73%; P = .001) in 2015 to 2018, and 21.71% (95% CI, 17.74% to 29.57%; P &amp;lt; .001) in 2019 to 2023. Baseline nonsurgical management increased with age, from 1331 of 19 785 patients younger than 50 years (6.73%) to 1748 of 6210 patients aged 80 years and older (28.15%). Earlier adoption occurred in older patients; the group aged 80 years and older surpassed 5–percentage point excess watch and wait by 2015 (33.78% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [5.63–percentage point excess]) and 10% by 2017 (39.56% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [11.41–percentage point excess]), compared with 2019 (12.88% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [6.15–percentage point excess]) and 2021 (20.75% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [14.02%] excess) in patients younger than 50 years. Overall, watch and wait increased from 140 of 6101 patients (2.30%) in 2015 to 2068 of 6280 patients (32.94%) in 2023. Increasing year (odds ratio for 2023 vs 2006, 6.23; 95% CI, 5.48 to 7.09) and older age (odds ratio for ages ≥80 vs &amp;lt;50 years, 4.25; 95% CI, 3.98 to 4.54) were independently associated with nonsurgical management (both P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this study, watch-and-wait rates increased across all age groups, with a marked acceleration after 2019 suggesting evidence-concordant adoption of the watch-and-wait approach. This underscores the need for careful patient selection, accurate clinical response assessment, and rigorous surveillance monitoring to ensure safe oncologic outcomes.

item.title: Bias-Adjusted Prevalence of Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Among Deceased National Football League Players
item.dc:creator: Julia Gallini
Michael L. Alosco
Bobak Abdolmohammadi
Jennifer Weuve
Ann C. McKee
Thor D. Stein
Robert A. Stern
Daniel H. Daneshvar
item.description:
Authors: Julia Gallini, Michael L. Alosco, Bobak Abdolmohammadi, Jennifer Weuve, Ann C. McKee, Thor D. Stein, Robert A. Stern, Daniel H. Daneshvar, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640884
Abstract: Importance The majority of knowledge regarding chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in National Football League (NFL) players is derived from autopsy-based studies on voluntarily donated brains. Because these cohorts are highly vulnerable to selection bias (specifically registry bias), population-level prevalence of CTE among former NFL players is unknown, limiting understanding of the impact of this disease. Objective To estimate the selection-bias adjusted prevalence of CTE neuropathology in deceased NFL players. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based cross-sectional study used Understanding Neurologic Injury and Traumatic Encephalopathy (UNITE) brain bank data combined with National Death Index records on former NFL players. Both brain donor and nondonor NFL players who died between January 2008 and December 2023 were included. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to April 2026. Exposure Playing in at least 1 regular or postseason NFL game. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes of this study were bias-adjusted prevalence of CTE neuropathology and all-cause dementia among the target population, both of which were measured in donors prior to this study. A cognitive symptom–related brain donation selection ratio (probability of donation given CTE divided by the probability of donation given no CTE) was estimated using Poisson regression and was applied to adjust donor-observed prevalence of CTE neuropathology at death and all-cause dementia during life. The prevalence estimates were adjusted for bias using the estimated selection ratio. Results The cohort consisted of 2362 deceased former NFL players (mean [SD] years played, 5.1 [3.9]; 971 [41.1%] aged ≥80 years at death), of whom 396 were brain donors and 1966 were nondonors. Of 387 donors, 362 (93.5%) had CTE. The median selection ratio was 4.97 (95% CI, 4.72-5.26). Bias-adjusted population prevalence of CTE at death was 74.5% (95% CI, 69.6%-78.3%), with a conservative lower-bound analysis estimating 63.7% (57.2%-68.9%). Bias-adjusted population prevalence of all-cause dementia history during life was 27.2% (95% CI, 22.6%-31.6%). Conclusions and Relevance The findings of this cross-sectional study suggest that selection bias materially inflates donor-based prevalence estimates but is unlikely to fully explain the high burden of CTE neuropathology among this population. Further research is required to understand the clinical impact of this disease.

item.title: Effectiveness of the mRNA-1345 Vaccine Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus in US Veterans
item.dc:creator: David P. Bui
Lei Yan
Yuli Li
Nallakkandi Rajeevan
Robert Vergun
Vyshnika Sriskantharajah
Denise M. Hynes
Kristin Berry
item.description:
Authors: David P. Bui, Lei Yan, Yuli Li, Nallakkandi Rajeevan, Robert Vergun, Vyshnika Sriskantharajah, Denise M. Hynes, Kristin Berry, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640981
Abstract: Importance In clinical trials, the messenger RNA (mRNA)–1345 vaccine provided protection against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) illness. Data on mRNA-1345 effectiveness in broader patient populations are needed. Objective To estimate the effectiveness of mRNA-1345 vaccination during a single respiratory illness season. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used a target trial emulation framework to assess veterans 50 years and older receiving care in the Veterans Health Administration. Eligible vaccine recipients were matched with up to 4 unvaccinated individuals in 4 monthly, nested, sequential trials from October 1, 2025, to January 31, 2026. Outcomes were ascertained through May 31, 2026, or 24 weeks. Exposure A single dose of mRNA-1345 RSV vaccine vs no RSV vaccination. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was any positive RSV test result from day 14 after the matched index date. Secondary outcomes included RSV-associated emergency department (ED) or urgent care (UC) encounters and RSV-associated hospitalizations. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated as 100 × (1 – risk ratio). A sensitivity analysis comparing veterans who received same-day mRNA-1345 and influenza vaccination to influenza vaccination alone (active comparator arm) was performed to explore potential bias from differences in health care–seeking behavior and outcome ascertainment between comparator groups. Results A total of 74 926 vaccinated veterans were matched to 286 425 unique control individuals, weighted to represent 74 926 individuals, for a total of 149 852 study participants (median [IQR] age, 73.0 [63.3-78.6] years; 136 756 [91.3%] male). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 160 (130-168) days, estimated vaccine effectiveness was 60.3% (95% CI, 49.0%-70.4%) against any documented infection, 60.2% (95% CI, 47.2%-71.5%) against RSV-associated ED or UC encounters, and 81.8% (95% CI, 58.1%-99.9%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations. Estimated effectiveness against documented infections decreased with increasing age, from 82.9% (95% CI, 64.0%-96.7%) in the 50- to 59-year age group to 28.6% (95% CI, −12.0% to 60.4%) in the 80-year or older age group. With an active comparator arm, estimated effectiveness was 67.1% (95% CI, 48.9%-82.6%) against documented RSV infections, 69.5% (95% CI, 49.7%-85.4%) against RSV-associated ED and UC encounters, and 86.9% (95% CI, 56.5%-100.0%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study using a target trial emulation of mRNA-1345 vaccine effectiveness during 24 weeks, vaccination was associated with protection against RSV illness and associated health care use in adults 50 years and older. Comparative effectiveness studies are needed to determine the relative benefits of available RSV vaccine products.

item.title: Exercise Training During Neoadjuvant Treatment for Gastroesophageal Cancer and Tumor Surgery
item.dc:creator: Casper Simonsen
Pieter de Heer
Simon Nørskov Thomsen
Rikke Krabek
Sarah Thorsen-Streit
Mark Preben Printz Lyngbæk
Anna Sundberg
Anne Sofie Knust Hjort
item.description:
Authors: Casper Simonsen, Pieter de Heer, Simon Nørskov Thomsen, Rikke Krabek, Sarah Thorsen-Streit, Mark Preben Printz Lyngbæk, Anna Sundberg, Anne Sofie Knust Hjort, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640136
Abstract: Importance Physical deterioration and disease progression during neoadjuvant treatment can preclude tumor surgery in patients with gastroesophageal cancer. Whether preoperative exercise training can increase the probability of undergoing tumor surgery remains unknown. Objective To compare exercise training with usual care on the likelihood of not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent after neoadjuvant treatment for gastroesophageal cancer. Design, Setting, and Participants PRESET-RCT was a single-blinded, parallel-group, 2-arm, superiority randomized clinical trial. Patients with gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma scheduled to undergo treatment with curative intent, including neoadjuvant treatment, and with no contraindication to exercise training were eligible. Participants were enrolled at University Hospital Copenhagen, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, Denmark, from August 16, 2018, to September 23, 2022, with final follow-up on October 22, 2024. Data analysis was performed from March 2023 to May 2025. Intervention The participants were randomized 1:1 to preoperative exercise training from diagnosis until tumor surgery or control. The intervention consisted of twice-weekly concurrent aerobic exercise and resistance training. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent. The secondary outcomes were treatment tolerance and overall survival. Results In total, 207 participants (73.7%) were randomized and 202 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analyses (mean [SD] age, 65.3 [8.5] years; 161 [78.9%] male; 170 [83.3%] with gastroesophageal junction cancer), with 101 randomized to each group. In the exercise group, 10 (9.9%) did not undergo tumor surgery with curative intent compared with 8 (7.9%) in the control group (odds ratio, 1.28; 95% CI, 0.48-3.38; P = .62). There were no between-group differences in permanent discontinuation of neoadjuvant treatment (odds ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.38-1.72) or postoperative complications (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.61-2.20). The overall survival rates at 3 years for the exercise and control group were 51.0% and 65.0%, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.02-2.45). Conclusion and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, preoperative exercise training did not increase the likelihood of undergoing tumor surgery for patients with gastroesophageal cancer. The findings do not support the use of exercise training during neoadjuvant treatment to improve surgical outcomes, and further research is needed to determine its effects on long-term outcomes. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03490565

item.title: Annual Wellness Visits and New Dementia Medication Prescriptions Among US Medicare Beneficiaries
item.dc:creator: Sadaf Arefi Milani
Yong-Fang Kuo
Yong Shan
Eunice Park
Abisola Sotade
Huey-Ming Tzeng
Mukaila Raji
item.description:
Authors: Sadaf Arefi Milani, Yong-Fang Kuo, Yong Shan, Eunice Park, Abisola Sotade, Huey-Ming Tzeng, Mukaila Raji
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640804
Abstract: Importance Medicare annual wellness visits (AWVs) may facilitate early diagnosis of Alzheimer disease and related dementias (ADRDs). However, it remains unclear whether AWVs lead to increased new prescriptions of dementia medications, including N -methyl- d -aspartate receptor antagonists (memantine) and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine). Objective To examine the association between incident AWVs and new dementia medication prescriptions. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used 100% Medicare data for beneficiaries with ADRDs diagnosed from January 1 to December 31, 2018, who had continuous enrollment in Medicare Parts A, B, and D, from 3 years before to 1 year after the index date (January 1, 2018), excluding those enrolled in health maintenance organizations and with prior dementia medication prescriptions. Data analysis was performed from August 2025 to August 2026. Exposure Number of AWVs received in the 3 years before the index date (0, 1, 2, or ≥3). Main Outcomes and Measures Receipt of any dementia medication (yes or no). Results In this cohort of 799 268 Medicare beneficiaries with ADRDs (mean [SD] age, 82.3 [7.9] years; 64.5% female), 60.8% received no AWVs, 19.2% received 1 AWV, 12.9% received 2 AWVs, and 7.2% received 3 or more AWVs. New dementia medication prescriptions ranged from 9.8% to 14.1%, varying by number of AWVs received. After propensity score weighting, receipt of 1 AWV was associated with a 9.0% higher rate in dementia medication prescriptions (hazard ratio [HR], 1.09; 95% CI, 1.07-1.11), receipt of 2 AWVs was associated with a 12.0% higher rate (HR, 1.12; 95% CI, 1.10-1.14), and receipt of 3 or more AWVs was associated with a 16.0% higher rate (HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.13-1.19). An interaction between AWVs and prevalent cases of dementia was observed ( P for interaction = .009). For both incident and prevalent cases of dementia, a higher rate of dementia medications was associated with a higher number of AWVs, but those with incident dementia cases had larger increases. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries with ADRD, an increasing number of AWVs received was associated with higher rates of new dementia medication prescriptions. These findings underscore the important role that AWVs may have in increasing the prescribing of medications that help manage symptoms of ADRD and suggest AWVs are essential to support quality dementia care (eg, symptom management) and advance care planning for future living arrangements.

item.title: Operational Challenges During Public Health Emergencies in Safety-Net Hospitals
item.dc:creator: Tara Kirk Sell
Vanessa Grégoire
Madisen S. Neufeld
Rachel R. Adler
Geoffrey Gosselin
Alysa Pomer
Biak L. Tial
Joel S. Weissman
item.description:
Authors: Tara Kirk Sell, Vanessa Grégoire, Madisen S. Neufeld, Rachel R. Adler, Geoffrey Gosselin, Alysa Pomer, Biak L. Tial, Joel S. Weissman, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640799
Abstract: Importance Safety-net hospitals (SNHs) serve as essential public health hubs, providing direct clinical care and critical social services to vulnerable populations, yet gaps persist in their ability to reliably deliver these essential services during disasters. Objective To identify common challenges faced by SNHs and actionable approaches described by participants to strengthen future emergency response capacity at these critical institutions. Design, Setting, and Participants For this qualitative study, from April through November 2025, key informant interviews were conducted with individuals across SNHs selected to represent a spectrum of SNH types. Thematic analysis of site-level case studies was used to identify cross-cutting and context-specific patterns across 5 domains: load balancing, staffing needs, supply chain, crisis standards of care (CSC), and health care coalitions (HCCs). Main Outcomes and Measures Stakeholder perspectives of pandemic preparedness, response, and recovery were evaluated to understand strategies to mitigate future health care disasters. Results Analysis of interviews with 69 individuals from 10 SNH sites identified systemic vulnerabilities across all 5 domains in SNHs. SNHs rarely succeeded in transferring critically ill patients without extensive staff time spent setting up the transfer. SNHs often experienced severe workforce disruptions from limited staff pools and nurse attrition, leaving them dependent on temporary staff at higher costs. Just-in-time personal protective equipment procurement and constricted manufacturing supply chains created supply crises. Few SNHs implemented full CSC, but many worked to find creative solutions to prevent more extensive changes in care standards. Opinions on written CSC were mixed, with some preferring structured frameworks and others preferring flexibility. Experiences with HCCs varied widely, with SNHs embedded in well-resourced HCCs reporting better coordination and support. Conclusions and Relevance In this qualitative study of SNH preparedness and response, findings indicated that SNHs faced challenges with load balancing, supply chain, staffing, CSC, and HCCs. To address such challenges in the future, SNHs, regional coalitions, and the federal government should implement sustainable changes that can be rapidly brought to bear in an emergency. Potential solutions may have outsized benefit for SNHs; however, such solutions must be designed to be accessible to SNHs and feasible in these settings.

item.title: School Phone Bans and Adolescent Mental Health in Iceland
item.dc:creator: Elena Bonilla Aparicio
Berglind Sigmarsdottir
Erin Haskell
Ulyana Sirotina
Berglind Sveinbjornsdottir
Bryndis Bjork Asgeirsdottir
Heiddis Bjork Valdimarsdottir
Candice Lynn Odgers
item.description:
Authors: Elena Bonilla Aparicio, Berglind Sigmarsdottir, Erin Haskell, Ulyana Sirotina, Berglind Sveinbjornsdottir, Bryndis Bjork Asgeirsdottir, Heiddis Bjork Valdimarsdottir, Candice Lynn Odgers, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640893
Abstract: Importance Concerns about adolescent smartphone use and mental health have prompted many schools to implement mobile phone bans, but evidence of their effects remains mixed. Objective To examine whether schoolwide mobile phone bans were associated with changes in mental health and associated social and behavioral outcomes among adolescents in Iceland. Design, Setting, and Participants This repeated cross-sectional study used difference-in-differences analyses of data from 70 schools across 3 waves of the nationwide Youth in Iceland school survey. The surveys were administered to adolescents aged 13 to 15 years in February 2016, February 2018, and November 2023. Analyses were conducted from February 1, 2025, to January 30, 2026. Exposure Schoolwide mobile phone bans prohibiting student phone use during school hours. Between 2018 and 2023, 22 of 70 schools implemented a phone ban. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were depressive symptoms, anxiety, hostility, and mental well-being. Secondary outcomes were perceived peer support, screen use (social media use, gaming alone, gaming with friends, and video watching), and bullying (in person and cyberbullying). Results Among 23 938 adolescent observations across the 3 study years, 11 964 (50.0%) were boys; the mean (SD) age was 13.98 (0.82) years. In the postpolicy period from 2018 to 2023, schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in depressive symptoms (β, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.01-1.30]), anxiety (β, 0.21 [95% CI, −0.08 to 0.50]), hostility (β, 0.23 [95% CI, −0.12 to 0.59]), and mental well-being (β, −0.52 [95% CI, −1.08 to 0.03]). Results were similar in gender-stratified analyses and for the secondary outcomes. Sensitivity analyses examining timing of implementation and more stringent phone restriction criteria were consistent with the main findings. Conclusions and Relevance In this repeated cross-sectional study of adolescents in Iceland, schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in adolescent mental health or related social and behavioral outcomes. These findings suggest that school phone bans implemented in isolation may be insufficient to improve adolescent mental health at the population level.

item.title: GLP-1 RA Prescribing in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Cancer
item.dc:creator: Xin Hu
Changchuan Jiang
Xuesong Han
Lu Zhang
Piaopiao Li
Francisco J. Pasquel
Jane L. Meisel
Jacqueline B. Vo
item.description:
Authors: Xin Hu, Changchuan Jiang, Xuesong Han, Lu Zhang, Piaopiao Li, Francisco J. Pasquel, Jane L. Meisel, Jacqueline B. Vo, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640781
Abstract: Importance Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are increasingly used to treat type 2 diabetes, yet little is known about its utilization patterns in patients with cancer history, given limited oncology-specific guidance. Objective To evaluate trends and factors associated with GLP-1 RA use among Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, comparing those with and without cancer history. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results–Medicare linked data to identify patients diagnosed with 7 common cancers in 2010 to 2021 and preexisting type 2 diabetes before cancer diagnosis. A noncancer cohort with type 2 diabetes was identified from a 5% random sample of Medicare beneficiaries and matched 1:1 to patients with cancer based on sociodemographic characteristics; controls were assigned a pseudo–index date corresponding to their matched patient’s cancer diagnosis date. Beneficiaries were followed up annually until death or December 31, 2022, for TM or December 31, 2021, for MA. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to July 2026. Exposures Diagnosis of 1 of 7 common cancers. Main Outcomes and Measures Any GLP-1 RA use. Proportions of beneficiaries with any GLP-1 RA use annually were stratified by traditional Medicare (TM) and Medicare Advantage (MA). Multivariable logistic regression examined (1) differences in GLP-1RA use between cancer and noncancer cohorts with and without adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics and comorbidities and diabetes-related complications; (2) cancer-specific factors associated with GLP-1RA use among the cancer cohort after 2018. Results A total of 373 278 Medicare beneficiaries (mean [SD] age, 76.1 [6.6] years; 188 746 [50.6%] female) with cancer and diabetes and 373 278 noncancer controls (153 358 unique beneficiaries) were included. GLP-1 RA use increased from 85 beneficiaries (0.5%) to 9083 beneficiaries (8.2%) and from 138 beneficiaries (0.9%) to 9300 beneficiaries (6.2%) in the cancer and noncancer cohorts, respectively, from 2010 to 2022 under TM; a similar increase was observed under MA. Despite higher unadjusted GLP-1 RA use among the cancer cohort than the noncancer cohort (probability difference, TM: 1.19 [95% CI, 0.94 to 1.44] percentage points [pp]; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 0.45 [95% CI, 0.21 to 0.68] pp, P &amp;lt; .001), adjusted analysis showed no significant differences in GLP-1 RA use under TM (adjusted probability difference, 0.16 [95% CI, −0.10 to 0.41,] pp; P = .22) and lower use among cancer cohort under MA (−0.52 [95% CI, −0.76 to −0.28] pp; P &amp;lt; .001). Complications or comorbidities, including obesity (adjusted probability difference, TM: 3.35 [95% CI, 3.10 to 3.61] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 2.42 [95% CI, 2.19 to 2.64] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), dyslipidemia (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.26 [95% CI, 2.03 to 2.50] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.80 [95% CI, 1.57 to 2.03] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), neuropathy (adjusted probability difference: TM: 3.91 [95% CI, 3.64 to 4.19] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 3.17 [95% CI, 2.94 to 3.41] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), retinopathy (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.02 [95% CI, 1.78 to 2.27] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.84 [95% CI, 1.63 to 2.06] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), and chronic kidney disease (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.01 [95% CI, 1.76 to 2.26] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.63 [95% CI, 1.40 to 1.85] pp; P &amp;lt; .001) were associated with greater likelihood of GLP-1RA use. Within the cancer cohort, breast (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.05 [95% CI, 0.43 to 1.66] pp; P = .001; MA: 0.89 [95% CI, 0.37 to 1.41] pp; P = .001), gynecologic (adjusted probability difference, MA: 1.13 [95% CI, 0.45 to 1.81] pp; P = .001), and prostate (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.30 [95% CI, 0.72 to 1.88] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.07 [95% CI, 0.56 to 1.58] pp; P &amp;lt; .001) cancers were associated with higher GLP-1 RA use than colorectal cancer, while pancreatic cancer was associated with lower GLP-1 RA use (adjusted probability difference, TM: −2.55 [95% CI, −3.17 to −1.93] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: −1.64 [95% CI, −2.23 to −1.05] pp; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this retrospective study of Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 RA use increased substantially and primarily was associated with metabolic risk profile, with limited associations with cancer status. Variation across cancer types and stages suggests oncologic context may influence prescribing.

item.title: Simpson’s Paradox, Amyloid Paradox, and Racial Differences
item.dc:creator: Chengjie Xiong

item.description:
Authors: Chengjie Xiong, Jingqin Luo, Ruijin Lu, Sarah Hartz, Walter Kukull, Suzanne E. Schindler, Joyce E. Balls-Berry, Jason Hassenstab, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640868
Abstract: Importance The underlying mechanisms for the paradox of higher prevalence of dementia but lower prevalence of amyloid positivity in self-identified Black US residents than White US residents remain unknown and are important for designing and analyzing prevention and treatment trials of Alzheimer disease. Objective To assess whether the age of mean amyloid onset (AMAO) explains the paradox of the reported racial differences in dementia and amyloid positivity. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a retrospective, multicenter, longitudinal cohort study with harmonized amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) and clinical data from self-identified Black and White individuals who were middle-aged or older across 5 academic institutes in the US conducting studies of memory and aging. The study was conducted from June 2020 to March 2026. Exposures Self-identified race, vascular comorbidities, sex, age, educational attainment, and apolipoprotein E ε4 carrier status. Main Outcomes and Measures Amyloid PET centiloid and cognition measured as a global cognitive composite constructed by averaging z scores across at least 6 cognitive tests in self-identified Black and White participants. Both cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted to compare racial groups in amyloid burden and cognition. Data were also analyzed using propensity score–matching of 2:1 (White:Black) by main covariates. Results Of 2653 participants (mean [SD] age, 69.0 [8.8] years; 1574 [59.3%] female), 406 (15.3%) were Black and 2247 (84.7%) were White. Black participants had a delayed AMAO compared with White participants in the unmatched (83.86 [95% CI, 76.55-91.35] years vs 71.38 [95% CI, 67.74-73.17] years; difference, 12.48 [95% CI, 5.03-22.28 years) and covariate-matched (85.17 [95% CI, 80.16-91.38] years vs 72.61 [95% CI, 70.79-74.55] years; difference, 12.57 [95% CI, 7.25-19.54] years) analyses. Although Black participants had a lower overall prevalence of amyloid positivity than White participants (24.1% vs 31.7%, P = .002), they had a higher prevalence of amyloid positivity than White participants in almost every interval of expected years to amyloid onset (EYAO, defined as participants’ simple chronological age minus the group-specific AMAO), hence Simpson’s paradox, (eg, −15 to −10 years for Black minus White prevalence in the unmatched cohort, 15.30 percentage points [95% Wilson CI, 0.06-0.26]). No significant racial differences were found in the longitudinal rate of amyloid accumulation after adjusting for the covariates either before the AMAO (eg, unmatched cohort Black minus White difference in slope per year, −0.28 [95% CI, −0.64 to 0.08]; P = .13) or after the AMAO (eg, unmatched cohort Black minus White difference in slope, −1.23 [95% CI, −3.05 to 0.60]; P = .17). Black participants had a higher prevalence of vascular comorbidities than White participants (56.9% vs 39.3%; P &amp;lt; .001), and Black but not White participants showed significant cognitive decline before the AMAO (Black minus White difference in slope per year, −0.016 (95% CI, −0.028 to −0.004)]; P = .009). Conclusions and Relevance This cohort study found that Black participants had delayed AMAO compared with White participants, partially explaining the paradox of the reported racial differences in prevalence of amyloid positivity and dementia. This finding suggests that EYAO may be an important confounder to analyze racial differences and may serve as a better (than age) inclusion or exclusion criterion to improve the representation of Black US residents in clinical trials of Alzheimer disease.

item.description:
Authors: Chu Chen, Jairo H. Migueles, Viktor H. Ahlqvist, Pablo Campos-Garzón, Pontus Henriksson, Martin Neovius, Maria Rosaria Galanti, Kyriaki Kosidou, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640617
Abstract: Importance Evidence regarding the effectiveness of physical activity (PA) policies within preschool settings remains limited. Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of a cocreated preschool-level PA policy on children’s accelerometer-measured PA during preschool hours. Design, Setting, and Participants This single-blind, parallel-group, cluster randomized clinical trial was performed at public preschools in Stockholm, Sweden. Of 156 randomly sampled preschools invited, 124 were randomized. Children aged 3 to 5 years with parental consent were recruited from September 14 to December 11, 2020, baseline measurements from September 23, 2020, to January 22, 2021, and 6-month follow-up from March 8 to June 11, 2021. Statistical analyses were performed from March 6, 2023, to October 25, 2024. Intervention A cocreated preschool-level PA policy implemented for 6 months vs usual practice. Main Outcomes and Measures Prespecified primary outcomes were between-group differences in change in moderate to vigorous PA, total PA, and steps during preschool hours, measured using wearable accelerometers. Results Among 3751 children (mean [SD] age, 4.44 [0.86] years; 1934 male [51.6%]), 1960 attended intervention preschools and 1791 attended control preschools. All 124 preschools completed follow-up; data were available for 1530 children (78.1%) in intervention schools at baseline and 1435 (73.2%) at follow-up and 1430 children (79.8%) in control schools at baseline and 1356 (75.7%) at follow-up. Intention-to-treat analyses included 3417 children (1770 intervention and 1647 control). Moderate to vigorous PA increased from 27.4 to 33.0 minutes per day in the intervention group and from 27.6 to 33.0 minutes per day in the control group (difference in change, 0.3 [95% CI, −0.7 to 1.3] minutes per day; P = .57). Total PA increased from 177.7 to 185.3 minutes per day in the intervention group and from 176.5 to 184.5 minutes per day in the control group (difference, −0.3 [95% CI, −3.3 to 2.7] minutes per day; P = .84). Steps increased from 5415 to 5953 per day in the intervention and from 5549 to 6078 per day in the control groups (difference, 8 [95% CI, −118 to 133] steps per day; P = .90). No participants withdrew because of adverse events. Conclusions and Relevance In this cluster randomized clinical trial, a cocreated preschool PA policy did not increase children’s PA beyond usual practice after 6 months. These findings highlight the complexity of translating policy adoption into measurable behavioral change and of detecting such change in preschool settings. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04569578

item.title: Prescribing SGLTis and GLP-1 RAs for Patients With Type 2 Diabetes, Guideline Updates, and Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment Scores
item.dc:creator: Bradley M. Gray
Jonathan Vandergrift
Bruce E. Landon
Rozalina McCoy
item.description:
Authors: Bradley M. Gray, Jonathan Vandergrift, Bruce E. Landon, Rozalina McCoy
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640858
Abstract: Importance Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce cardiovascular and kidney events in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) who have established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, yet prescribing to these patients remains low. Objectives To describe temporal patterns in SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA prescribing before and after the 2019 American Diabetes Association (ADA) guideline update and to assess whether these patterns differed across physicians with subsequently measured different first-year American Board of Internal Medicine Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment (LKA) scores. Design, Setting, and Participants This serial cross-sectional study was conducted from October 2025 through January 2026, using 2017 to 2022 traditional Medicare claims. Endocrinologists first participating in the 2022 to 2023 LKA and the Medicare beneficiaries with T2D they treated were included. Exposure Time relative to the 2019 ADA guideline update. Main Outcomes and Measures The annual patient-year SGLT2i and GLP-1RA guideline-targeted and nontargeted patient fill rates were the main outcome. Linear physician, year, and target subgroup fixed-effects regression models were estimated, with patient demographic and health risk controls to evaluate within-physician associations between guideline-targeted vs nontargeted patient-year fill rates each year relative to 2018 (the year before the guideline update). The variation in these associations across first-year LKA score quartiles was also evaluated. Results A total of 1061 endocrinologists caring for 177 284 Medicare beneficiaries with T2D (mean [SD] age, 74.5 [6.1] years; mean [SD] 54.4% [49.8] female; mean [SD] 9.3% [29.1] Black, 6.6% [24.9] Hispanic, and 76.2% [42.6] White non-Hispanic) were included. Adjusted guideline-targeted SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA fill rates increased monotonically from 2018 to 2022 by 11.4 percentage points (pp) (95% CI, 10.5 to 12.3 pp; P &amp;lt; .001) and 2.4 (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.3 pp; P &amp;lt; .001) for SGLT2is and GLP-1 RAs targeted vs nontargeted subgroups, respectively. The associated SGLT2i increase was 3.9 pp (95% CI, 1.4 to 6.5 pp) larger for patients of endocrinologists with top vs bottom LKA quartile scores ( P = .003), but for GLP-1 RAs, this association was not statistically significant with wide confidence intervals. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study, 2019 ADA guideline update timing was associated with substantially increased SGLT2i and moderately increased GLP-1 RA guideline-concordant prescribing among guideline-targeted, compared with nontargeted, patient subgroups by 2020. These increases in SGLT2i guideline congruent prescribing were associated with higher subsequently measured first-year LKA scores.

item.title: Food Insecurity Among Resident Physicians and Clinical Fellows at a Large Academic Medical Center
item.dc:creator: Erin Mahan
Atalay Demiray
Stephen J. Huot
June Criscione
Marietta Vazquez
item.description:
Authors: Erin Mahan, Atalay Demiray, Stephen J. Huot, June Criscione, Marietta Vazquez
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640774
Abstract: Importance Food insecurity is associated with adverse health and affects approximately 1 in 5 US medical students. A recent multi-institutional study found food insecurity in 14% of graduate medical education trainees using a 2-item screen; prevalence by the 10-item US Department of Agriculture Adult Food Security Survey Module remains poorly characterized. Objective To estimate reported food insecurity prevalence among resident physicians and clinical fellows and identify affected subgroups and barriers. Design, Setting, and Participants In this cross-sectional, anonymous electronic survey at the Yale New Haven Health System, all physicians in accredited postgraduate training were eligible (approximately 600). The survey was fielded August 7, 2023, to May 19, 2026, and responses arrived through November 2025 (121 of 165 [73%] in 2023). Exposures Year of training (including postgraduate year 1 [PGY-1] status) and self-reported barriers to obtaining food. Main Outcomes and Measures Food insecurity, a score of 3 or higher on the 10-item US Department of Agriculture module; prevalences and associations reported with 95% CIs. Results Of approximately 600 eligible trainees, 165 (28%) participated; 164 had complete food security data (53 PGY-1, 34 PGY-2, 23 PGY-3, 32 PGY-4, 22 other, including fellows). Overall, 50 of 164 respondents (30.5%; 95% CI, 24.0%-37.9%) met criteria for food insecurity. PGY-1 prevalence (24 of 53 [45.3%]) was approximately twice that of later years (26 of 111 [23.4%]; odds ratio [OR], 2.71; 95% CI, 1.35-5.43; P = .004). Lack of money was associated with food insecurity (45 of 60 [75.0%] vs 4 of 100 [4.0%]; OR, 72.00; 95% CI, 22.61-229.30; P &amp;lt; .001), whereas lack of time was not (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.61-2.49; P = .55). PGY-1 trainees more often endorsed lack of money (27 of 52 [51.9%] vs 33 or 108 [30.6%]; OR, 2.45; 95% CI, 1.24-4.85; P = .009). Prevalence by specialty ranged from 5 of 26 (19.2%) to 5 of 10 (50.0%) ( P = .24). Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of 164 resident physicians and clinical fellows, approximately one-third of respondents reported food insecurity, with the highest burden among PGY-1 trainees, whose recall window spanned the transition from medical school into residency, and an association with lack of money. Financial supports targeted to that transition warrant prospective evaluation.

item.title: Enteric Fever and Antimicrobial Resistance
item.dc:creator: Christan H. Stager
Layne Dorough
Molly Steele
Felicita Medalla
Jared L. Reynolds
Kristen Heitzinger
Hayat Caidi
Kaitlin A. Tagg
item.description:
Authors: Christan H. Stager, Layne Dorough, Molly Steele, Felicita Medalla, Jared L. Reynolds, Kristen Heitzinger, Hayat Caidi, Kaitlin A. Tagg, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640971
Abstract: Importance Increasing antibiotic resistance in enteric fever (typhoid or paratyphoid fever) is a global public health threat. Knowledge of current antimicrobial resistance patterns and identification of factors associated with acquiring resistant infections can help inform treatment and prevention decisions. Objective To estimate the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant enteric fever in the US after the emergence of extensively drug-resistant Salmonella enterica Typhi in 2016 and describe characteristics of patients with resistant Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi strains. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional, laboratory-based study included cases of culture-confirmed enteric fever diagnosed in the US. From January 2016 to December 2020, US health departments submitted epidemiologic data to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) through the National Typhoid and Paratyphoid Fever Surveillance (NTPFS) system, and public health laboratories submitted the corresponding Typhi or Paratyphi isolates to the CDC through the National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System (NARMS). Initial data analysis was complete by March 31, 2023, and the antimicrobial resistance trends analysis was updated in August 2026. Exposures Patient variables collected by the NTPFS, including demographic characteristics, travel history, and typhoid vaccination status. Main Outcome and Measures Linked NTPFS-NARMS data from 2016 to 2020 were used to calculate the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance stratified by serotype and to conduct univariable logistic regression to estimate the associations of case characteristics and exposure variables with odds of infection with resistant strains. Results In this analysis, 2342 cases were included (1784 typhoid [76.2%], 426 paratyphoid A [18.2%], 114 paratyphoid B [4.9%], and 14 paratyphoid C [0.6%]; 4 isolates [0.2%] had unspecified paratyphoid serotypes). The median patient age was 25 years (IQR, 11-37 years), and patients were male in 1215 of 2325 cases (52.3%). Most patients reported traveling or residing internationally within 30 days of illness onset (1853 of 2217 [81.9%]). From 2016 to 2020, 1635 enteric fever isolates underwent susceptibility testing through NARMS; most Typhi (1061 of 1354 [78.4%]) and Paratyphi A (258 of 274 [94.2%]) isolates were not susceptible to ciprofloxacin. Among 1354 Typhi isolates, resistance exceeded 15% for ampicillin, for chloramphenicol, and for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and was 5.5% (74 isolates) for ceftriaxone; 1 Typhi isolate (0.1%) was resistant to azithromycin. Resistance to these agents was not observed among Paratyphi isolates. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study, most typhoid and paratyphoid infections were not susceptible to ciprofloxacin, suggesting that ciprofloxacin should be avoided as empiric therapy for most travel-associated enteric fever cases. Cases of ceftriaxone-resistant typhoid fever were also observed. These findings suggest that treatment of enteric fever should be tailored to susceptibility test results.

item.title: The Kaiser Permanente Research Bank as a Genomic Data Resource
item.dc:creator: Sarah Rowell
Yambazi Banda
Alan Bauck
Aldwin Carino
Justin Chan
Terrence Chinn
Elaine Chung
Madhavan Ganesh
item.description:
Authors: Sarah Rowell, Yambazi Banda, Alan Bauck, Aldwin Carino, Justin Chan, Terrence Chinn, Elaine Chung, Madhavan Ganesh, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640691
Abstract: Importance Large biobanks have become significant engines of discovery-based health research; the collection of large-scale genetic and other molecular data from a deeply phenotyped cohort enables epidemiological studies, biomarker discovery, predictive modeling, and health economic research. In many biobanks, participant data collection is cross-sectional and relies on self-reported medical histories. Furthermore, biobanks may lack ancestral diversity and may need to be enriched for healthy individuals with lower rates of chronic disease. Objective To describe the scope and purpose of the Kaiser Permanente Research Bank (KPRB), a large biobank created from medical records, health and socioeconomic surveys, genomic data, and biospecimens of the Kaiser Permanente patient population. Observations The KPRB was intended to compile longitudinal medical records data and build a biospecimen collection that included a patient population that was wide and diverse, enabling a wide variety of research pursuits. KPRB participant medical records, survey data, and biospecimens were compiled to enable researcher use. Genomic DNA from participant samples were genotyped and these data were used in genome-wide association studies of blood pressure phenotypes. The KPRB achieved its goal of recruiting and consenting 400 000 participants (449 122 in total) and making available to the broader research community the participant data collected. The KPRB’s comprehensive medical records extend retrospectively up to 28 years (median [IQR], 20.9 [14.0-28.7] years) and continue to accumulate patient data for as long as a participant is a KP member. KPRB participants represent a diversity of race and ethnicity groups (38 209 Asian [8.5%], 26 106 Black [5.8%], 50 661 Hispanic [11.3%], 317 630 White [70.7%]) and health outcomes, including both prevalent disease at the time of recruitment and incident disease diagnosed postrecruitment, that are typical of US-based populations. Genomic data collected on nearly all participants has been quality controlled and subjected to imputation. A new genome-wide association study (GWAS) analysis of blood pressure phenotypes in all genotyped KPRB participants has been conducted to validate previously published associations and confirm the quality of both the genomic and medical records data in the KPRB. Conclusions and Relevance The KPRB, with genetic data generated on a large and diverse cohort with comprehensive medical records, survey data, and biospecimens, will support the growing interest in large biobank-based research and enable new avenues of research. GWAS analyses of common phenotypes measured as part of routine medical care indicated that KPRB is a robust resource linking health outcomes with genetic data that will yield valuable research findings. Access to the KPRB resource is available to external researchers with compelling research proposals through KPRB’s Access Review Committee.

item.title: Stroke and Bleeding Risk in Long-Term Care Residents With Atrial Fibrillation Who Discontinue Anticoagulation
item.dc:creator: Alok Kapoor
Zhiyong Chen
Jay Patel
Zehao Ye
Honghuang Lin
Geoffrey Barnes
Sybil Crawford
Jerry H. Gurwitz
item.description:
Authors: Alok Kapoor, Zhiyong Chen, Jay Patel, Zehao Ye, Honghuang Lin, Geoffrey Barnes, Sybil Crawford, Jerry H. Gurwitz
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640964
Abstract: Importance Atrial fibrillation (AF) leads to more than 100 000 cases of stroke yearly and is particularly prevalent in long-term care (LTC) residents. Anticoagulation (AC) is the mainstay of stroke prevention, but given its risks, clinicians and residents may consider discontinuation at the time of LTC entry. Objective To estimate the association between AC discontinuation and stroke and bleeding risk among LTC residents with AF. Design, Setting, and Participants This comparative effectiveness research study with target trial emulation used claims data (2020-2021) from LTC facilities in the US serving Medicare beneficiaries. Medicare beneficiaries with AF receiving AC who entered LTC between April 1 and December 31, 2020, were included; those with additional indications for AC, including prosthetic heart valve or venous thromboembolism, were excluded. Analysis was performed in August 2026. Exposure Discontinuer vs continuer assignment. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes were stroke (including ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, and systemic embolism) and bleeding, assessed using Medicare claims. A target trial emulation was conducted with clone censor weighting (CCW) analysis. Specifically, eligible LTC residents were assigned (cloned) to each of 2 strategies: AC discontinuation or AC continuation. Clones were then censored when they deviated from their assigned strategy, and inverse probability of censoring weighting was applied to address informative censoring: residents who deviated differing systematically from those who did not. Subdistribution hazard ratios (sHRs) for stroke and bleeding were then calculated to account for competing mortality and a cause-specific hazard ratio (HR) for death. Results This study included 15 426 LTC residents (mean [SD] age, 82.6 [7.6] years). Most were female (62.6%). AC discontinuers had 187 strokes, 297 bleeding events, and 3684 deaths over a mean (SD) of 128.9 (177.9) days. AC continuers had 321 strokes, 493 bleeding events, and 5475 deaths over a mean (SD) of 279.6 (204.9) days. Discontinuers had similar stroke risk (sHR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.93-1.23) and bleeding risk (sHR, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.92-1.13) compared with continuers, but discontinuers had higher mortality risk (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.23-1.31). Conclusions and Relevance In this target trial emulation with CCW in a cohort of LTC residents with AF, AC discontinuation was not associated with higher stroke or bleeding risk. Very high mortality, unmeasured confounding, and reliance on claims-based outcome ascertainment may have limited the ability to better understand the consequences of AC discontinuation on stroke and bleeding.

item.title: Cancer Screening, Diagnosis, and Survival in California Prisons
item.dc:creator: Christopher R. Manz
Angela C. Tramontano
Emma Voligny
Samira L. Dias
Marcus Dahlstrom
John Dunlap
Amanda Johnson
Vikrant Dev Rathore
item.description:
Authors: Christopher R. Manz, Angela C. Tramontano, Emma Voligny, Samira L. Dias, Marcus Dahlstrom, John Dunlap, Amanda Johnson, Vikrant Dev Rathore, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640539
Abstract: Importance Cancer is the leading cause of death in prison. Limited literature suggests cancer screening rates in prison are low, but population-level screening data in prisons are scarce. Objective To determine screening rates for 5 cancer types, identify individual and incarceration characteristics associated with receipt of screening, and characterize outcomes for screen-detectable cancers in California prisons. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study included individuals incarcerated in California state prisons who were eligible for breast, cervical, colorectal, liver, or lung cancer screening between January 1, 2014, and June 30, 2023. Incarceration data were linked to state cancer registry data from 2014 to 2021 to identify screen-detectable cancers diagnosed in the study population. Analyses were conducted between August 2024 and July 2025. Exposures Receipt of screening within 3 months before a cancer diagnosis. Main Outcomes and Measures Receipt of cancer screening; screening rates; and cancer diagnosis, stage, and survival were calculated. Multivariable models evaluated characteristics associated with screening receipt and associations between screening receipt and stage at diagnosis and survival, with adjustment for demographic and incarceration characteristics. Results The study included 106 352 incarcerated individuals (median [IQR] age at first eligibility, 50 [47-55] years; 86 559 males [81.4%]). By June 30, 2023 (data cutoff), 89.4%, 81.2%, 80.0%, 70.1%, and 76.0% of individuals were up-to-date with screening for breast, colorectal, cervical, lung, and liver cancer screening, respectively. Characteristics associated with higher likelihood of ever receiving screening included mental health service use, prison security level 3 or 4, recent change in primary care practitioner, and incarceration within the past year before screening eligibility. Of 812 patients with screening data, 92 (11.3%) were diagnosed with screen-detectable cancer before they met eligibility for screening, including 56 with liver cancer. A total of 392 screening-eligible patients (48.3%) were diagnosed with screen-detectable cancer while in prison during the study period. Approximately 71% of patients received screening within 3 months before diagnosis, which was associated with lower odds of stage IV disease at diagnosis (odds ratio, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.23-0.85) and better survival (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.44-0.88); rates of stage IV cancer were lower for individuals with recent screening than those without recent screening (10.0% vs 21.0%). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of incarcerated individuals in California prisons, screening rates were high and associated with early-stage cancer diagnoses, suggesting that effective cancer screening is achievable in prison settings. Future work should examine whether increased screening ameliorates incarceration-related cancer disparities.

item.title: Cancer Incidence and Survival Among Ever-Incarcerated Patients in California and Massachusetts
item.dc:creator: Christopher R. Manz
Angela C. Tramontano
Samira L. Dias
Emma Voligny
Christopher D. Baggett
Alexi A. Wright
Deborah Schrag
item.description:
Authors: Christopher R. Manz, Angela C. Tramontano, Samira L. Dias, Emma Voligny, Christopher D. Baggett, Alexi A. Wright, Deborah Schrag
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639346
Abstract: Importance Cancer is the leading cause of death in US prisons. Few studies have compared cancer incidence and survival for currently and formerly incarcerated populations with those for the general population. Objective To ascertain the association of prison incarceration with cancer outcomes, and to inform potential public health interventions. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used state cancer registry data on patients with cancer diagnosed in California and Massachusetts between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2019. Identifiers of persons incarcerated in California and Massachusetts state prisons during this study period were linked to cancer registry data to identify incarceration status at diagnosis. Data analysis was performed between March 2023 and August 2025. Exposures Current, former, or never incarceration status at diagnosis. Main Outcomes and Measures Cancer incidence, which was calculated as standardized incidence ratios (SIRs) relative to never-incarcerated patients. Stage at diagnosis and survival outcomes were characterized. The association between incarceration status and diagnosis stage and survival were assessed using regression models adjusted for demographic characteristics, year of diagnosis, cancer type, and state of residence. Results The study included 2 171 336 cancers, among which 2 165 540 (99.7%) were diagnosed in never-incarcerated, 3305 (0.2%) in currently incarcerated, and 2491 (0.1%) in formerly incarcerated patients. The median (IQR) age at diagnosis was 66 (56-75) years, 57 (49-64) years, and 55 (46-62) years, respectively. Overall, patients included 1 141 745 males (52.6%). Compared with never-incarcerated patients, currently incarcerated patients were more likely to have cervical (SIR, 3.57; 95% CI, 2.26-5.35) and liver cancers (SIR, 3.10; 95% CI, 2.79-3.43). In Massachusetts, currently incarcerated patients (odds ratio [OR], 1.62; 95% CI, 1.07-2.46) and all formerly incarcerated patients (OR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.02-1.38) had a higher likelihood of advanced-stage diagnoses of screen-detectable cancers. Five-year survival was 62.4% for all never-incarcerated patients, 54.4% for currently incarcerated patients in California, 36.4% for currently incarcerated patients in Massachusetts, and 51.8% for all formerly incarcerated patients. Compared with never-incarcerated patients, formerly incarcerated patients had worse adjusted survival (hazard ratio [HR], 1.71; 95% CI, 1.61-1.82), while currently incarcerated patients had worse survival that varied by state (California: HR, 1.41 [95% CI, 1.33-1.49]; Massachusetts: HR, 2.18 [95% CI, 1.85-2.56]). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of Massachusetts and California cancer registry data, currently and formerly incarcerated patients with cancer had inferior survival. The distinctive epidemiologic pattern of cancer incidence and mortality in incarcerated populations identifies strategic targets for cancer control.

item.title: Clinician Bias and Patient Experience in Cancer Genetic Counseling
item.dc:creator: Nao Hagiwara
Yongyun Shin
Sabina Yeasmin
Erin P. Carmany
Susan Eggly
Shown C. T. Jones
Nadia Harika
Anaya Gorham
item.description:
Authors: Nao Hagiwara, Yongyun Shin, Sabina Yeasmin, Erin P. Carmany, Susan Eggly, Shown C. T. Jones, Nadia Harika, Anaya Gorham, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639990
Abstract: Importance Genetic counseling helps reduce cancer burden; however, disparities exist in genetic counseling. Objective To examine associations between genetic counselor (GC) biases (implicit and/or explicit prejudice and stereotyping) and patient-centered outcomes in cancer genetic counseling. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a cohort study of patient-clinician communication during cancer genetic counseling focusing on hereditary cancer risk assessment. GCs and patients completed baseline surveys, video and/or audio-recorded sessions, and postencounter surveys. Data were collected at 2 comprehensive cancer centers in the South and Midwest, from August 3, 2023, to July 30, 2025. Exposure At baseline, GCs completed measures of implicit prejudice (Race Implicit Association Test), implicit stereotyping (Medical Cooperativeness Implicit Association Test), explicit prejudice (feeling thermometer), and explicit stereotyping (general and medical-context stereotype subscales). Main Outcomes and Measures Patients reported postencounter therapeutic alliance, satisfaction, and decisional conflicts. Differences between Black and White patients were evaluated using Welch t test for continuous variables and χ 2 or Fisher exact test for categorical variables. Hypothesis testing was conducted using linear mixed-effects models with GC-specific random effects and intracluster correlation coefficients. Results The current analysis included 185 cases with complete clinician baseline, patient baseline, and patient postencounter data. The 185 patients (mean [SD] age, 50.1 [14.0] years; 169 female [91.4%]; 16 male [8.6%]; 83 Black [44.9%]; 102 White [55.1%]) saw 1 of the 15 clinicians (mean [SD] age, 32.2 [9.5] years; 8 certified [53.3%]; 7 trainees [46.7%]). Among Black patients (mean [SD] age, 50.1 [13.6] years; 80 female [96.4%]; 3 male [3.5%]), stronger GC endorsement of explicit medical-context stereotypes favoring White over Black patients was significantly associated with poorer therapeutic alliance ( b [SE], −1.40 [0.37] to −1.54 [0.46]), lower satisfaction ( b [SE], −0.74 [0.27]), and greater decisional conflict ( b [SE], −0.85 [0.27] to −0.91 [0.25]), after covariate adjustment. Among White patients (mean [SD] age, 50.1 [14.4] years; 89 [87.3%] female; 13 [12.7%] male), no biases were significantly associated with outcomes after adjustment ( b [SE], −0.14 [0.49] to −0.48 [0.49]). Explicit medical-context stereotyping was the only factor significantly and consistently associated with racial disparities in patient-centered outcomes ( b [SE], −1.35 [0.49] to −1.93 [0.61]). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of cancer genetic counseling, stronger endorsement of medical-context stereotypes favoring White over Black patients was significantly associated with poorer patient-centered outcomes among Black patients. Explicit medical-context stereotypes may contribute to racial disparities in genetic counseling. Interventions should address explicit stereotyping and its role in clinical communication.

item.title: Maternal Vaccination vs Nirsevimab Use and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection Among Full-Term Infants
item.dc:creator: Karen B. Jacobson
Andrew J. Watson
Lauren D. Liao
Sally C. Stephens
Maqdooda Merchant
Ousseny Zerbo
Nicola P. Klein
item.description:
Authors: Karen B. Jacobson, Andrew J. Watson, Lauren D. Liao, Sally C. Stephens, Maqdooda Merchant, Ousseny Zerbo, Nicola P. Klein
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2636760
Abstract: Importance Since 2023, infants can be protected from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) through a vaccine (RSVpreF) for pregnant persons or a monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab) for infants. Objective To assess the relative product effectiveness (rPE) of maternal RSVpreF vs infant nirsevimab against RSV infection and hospitalization among infants born in the 2023 to 2025 RSV seasons. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study included full-term infants born at Kaiser Permanente Northern California (KPNC), an integrated health care system with approximately 40 000 births each year, from December 3, 2023, to March 30, 2024, or September 29, 2024, to March 15, 2025. Infants protected by RSVpreF were matched to infants protected with nirsevimab with optimal full matching (up to 1:5), adjusting for birth week, sex, and maternal factors. Each group was also compared with infants with no protection, matching unprotected infants to both RSVpreF and nirsevimab infants (up to 1:10). Exposures Maternal RSVpreF at 32 to 36 weeks’ gestation or infant nirsevimab through age 7 days. Main Outcomes and Measures Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)–confirmed RSV and RSV hospitalization (PCR-confirmed RSV 10 days before to 7 days after hospitalization) in infants aged 8 to 180 days or through RSV season end (April 30 in both seasons). rPE was estimated from age 8 to 180 days using restricted mean time lost. Results Of 15 124 matched infants (7729 [51.1%] male) in the primary analysis, 146 (0.97%) had RSV infection (106 of 11 293 [0.94%] in RSVpreF group and 40 of 3831 [1.04%] in nirsevimab group) and 12 (0.08%) were hospitalized (7 [0.06%] in RSVpreF group and 5 [0.13%] in nirsevimab group). The rPE of RSVpreF vs nirsevimab was −5.3% (95% CI, −44.8% to 23.4%) against infection and 61.5% (95% CI, −10.8% to 86.7%) against hospitalization. Compared with no protection, RSVpreF rPE was 69.3% (95% CI, 59.9% to 76.6%) against infection and 86.4% (95% CI, 66.4% to 94.5%) against hospitalization; nirsevimab rPE was 65.2% (95% CI, 51.0%-75.4%) and 73.8% (95% CI, 33.4%-89.7%), respectively. Conclusion In this cohort study of infants born in the 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025 RSV seasons, no statistically significant difference between maternal RSVpreF and infant nirsevimab in RSV infection or hospitalization was detected. Compared with no protection, both products were associated with fewer infections and hospitalizations. This study supports current US guidelines for either maternal RSVpreF or infant nirsevimab to protect all infants from RSV.

item.title: Longitudinal Change in Calf Circumference and Incident Falls in Older Adults
item.dc:creator: Chi Zhang
Ji Shen
Yushan Zhang
Zehong Huo
Yi Zeng
Jie Zhang
Yao Yao
item.description:
Authors: Chi Zhang, Ji Shen, Yushan Zhang, Zehong Huo, Yi Zeng, Jie Zhang, Yao Yao
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640127
Abstract: Importance Calf circumference (CC) is a simple, noninvasive proxy for lower-limb muscle mass. However, evidence on the longitudinal association between CC change and incident falls remains scarce. Objective To investigate whether progressive decline in CC is associated with higher odds of incident falls among community-dwelling older adults. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used data from the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey, a nationally representative prospective cohort. Participants aged 60 years or older with complete CC measurements at baseline (2018) and follow-up (2021) were included. Data were analyzed from January to March 2026. Exposures Absolute CC change (in centimeters) and relative CC change (as a percentage) over 3 years, analyzed as continuous and categorical variables (absolute: no decrease, &amp;lt;3 cm, 3 to &amp;lt;5 cm, ≥5 cm; relative: no decrease, &amp;lt;10%, 10% to &amp;lt;20%, ≥20%). The no-decrease group, including individuals with no change and those with increased CC, served as the reference group. Main Outcomes and Measures The outcome of interest was incident falls, self-reported during the 2021 wave. Covariates included sociodemographic characteristics, falls history, health behaviors, functional status, and chronic diseases, all assessed via standardized questionnaires and evaluation. Odds of incident fall were assessed using inverse probability weighted logistic regression to address survival bias. Results Among 7068 participants (mean [SD] age, 79.66 [10.32] years; 3835 [54.26%] female), 1671 participants (23.64%) reported incident falls over a median (IQR) follow-up of 3.07 (2.91-3.17) years. In fully adjusted models, each 1-cm absolute decrease in CC was associated with 3.2% higher odds of fall (odds ratio [OR], 1.03; 95% CI, 1.02-1.05) and each 10% relative decrease with 10.3% higher odds (OR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.06-1.15). Compared with no decrease, an absolute decrease in CC of 5 cm or more was associated with 32.5% higher odds of fall (OR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.10-1.60) and a relative decrease of 20% or more with 48.1% higher odds (OR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.20-1.84). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of older adults, longitudinal decreases in CC, both absolute and relative, were associated with higher odds of incident falls. Monitoring CC change over time may serve as a practical, low-cost measure to support fall risk assessment.

item.title: Ultraprocessed Food Intake, Striatal Response to Food Cues, and Adiposity Gain in Children
item.dc:creator: Jasmin M. Alves
Ella Morgan
Brendan Angelo
Kianna Le
Jared Smith
Ting Chow
Kay Jann
Anny H. Xiang
item.description:
Authors: Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, Jared Smith, Ting Chow, Kay Jann, Anny H. Xiang, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640252
Abstract: Importance Preclinical studies suggest that ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) are associated with increased dopaminergic signaling in the striatum, reinforcing intake. Whether habitual UPF consumption is associated with striatal responses to food cues and subsequent adiposity gain in children is unknown. Objective To examine associations between habitual UPF intake, striatal responses to food cues, and 1-year adiposity changes in children. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort study included children of healthy weight who were participating in the longitudinal BrainChild study. Baseline assessments were completed between April 11, 2015, and June 28, 2024, and included brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary recalls, and adiposity measurements. Additional follow-up assessments of adiposity were conducted 1 year later (April 18, 2016, to June 19, 2025). Exposure Habitual UPF intake, defined as the percentage of total energy intake from UPFs based on multiple 24-hour dietary recalls using the NOVA classification system. Main Outcomes and Measures Blood oxygenation level–dependent (BOLD) responses to food cues in the dorsal and ventral striatum during functional MRI and 1-year changes in body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and waist circumference. Associations were examined using linear regression models and adjusted for age, sex, baseline BMI, and total caloric intake, with regression coefficient (β) reported as per SD change in outcome with per SD change in the exposure variable. Results In 46 children of healthy weight (mean [SD] age, 8.7 [1.1] years; 26 [57%] female; baseline BMI range, 13.8-19.9; body fat percentage range, 12.7%-32.2%), higher habitual UPF consumption was associated with greater BOLD responses to food cues in the dorsal striatum (β = 0.34; 95% CI, 0.07-0.61) but not the ventral striatum (β = 0.16; 95% CI, −0.14 to 0.46). Greater dorsal striatal food cue responsivity was associated with 1-year increases in BMI (β = 0.32; 95% CI, 0.02-0.62) and body fat percentage (β = 0.44; 95% CI, 0.15-0.72). Baseline UPF intake was associated with a 1-year increase in waist circumference (β = 0.38; 95% CI, 0.11-0.66). Point estimates for associations between UPF intake and increases in BMI (β = 0.28; 95% CI, 0.00-0.57) and body fat percentage (β = 0.29; 95% CI, 0.00-0.57) were positive. Inclusion of dorsal striatal responsivity attenuated the UPF associations with 1-year change in BMI by 31% and with body fat percentage by 44%. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of children of healthy weight, higher habitual UPF intake was associated with greater dorsal striatal responses to food cues and prospective increases in adiposity. These findings suggest that reward-related brain responses may be involved in associations between UPF consumption and adiposity gain during childhood.

item.dc:creator: Qaidar Alizai

Areesh Mevawalla
Rida Ejaz
Jethro Wang Zih-shou
Meher Angez
Abdulaziz Elemosho

item.description:
Authors: Qaidar Alizai, Lorenza Arena, Areesh Mevawalla, Rida Ejaz, Jethro Wang Zih-shou, Meher Angez, Abdulaziz Elemosho, Charalampos M. Charalampous, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640261
Abstract: Importance The Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded insurance coverage, while the 2018 Public Charge Rule Proposal (PCRP) raised concerns about immigration-related barriers to health care access. Objective To evaluate changes in insurance coverage, health care use, and medical expenditures among immigrant and US-born adults across ACA expansion and post-PCRP eras, stratified by poverty status. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (2010-2023) data for US adults aged 19 to 64 years with available data on nativity, family income, insurance coverage, use, and expenditures. Income less than 138% of the federal poverty level was considered low income; 138% or higher was considered not low. Data were analyzed from April 1, 2026, to April 15, 2026. Exposures Policy era, categorized as pre–ACA expansion (2010-2013), post–ACA expansion (2014-2018), and post-PCRP (2019-2023), and nativity, categorized as immigrant or US-born. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were person-year measures of insurance coverage, health care use, and annual medical expenditures adjusted to constant 2023 US dollars. Survey-weighted multivariable models estimated adjusted changes across eras and tested differences by nativity. Results Complete-case adjusted analyses included 237 175 person-year observations from 126 724 unique adults, including 67 076 female adults (50.8%) and 59 648 male adults (49.2%), with a survey-weighted mean (SD) age of 40.8 (13.2) years; the analytic sample included 56 561 low-income and 180 614 non–low-income person-year observations. Among adults with low income, post-PCRP insurance coverage was higher among US-born adults (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 2.84; 95% CI, 2.55-3.17) and immigrants (AOR, 2.29; 95% CI, 1.98-2.65), with smaller relative gains for immigrants. Post-PCRP total expenditures increased among US-born adults with low income (β = $1684.60; 95% CI, $883.10-$2486.20) but not among immigrants with low income (β = $220.20; 95% CI, −$680.10-$1120.50). Among adults without low income, post-PCRP total expenditures increased among US-born adults (β = $1788.60; 95% CI, $1487.70-$2089.50) and immigrants (β = $974.10; 95% CI, $517.50-$1430.70). Conclusions and Relevance In this serial cross-sectional study of US adults aged 19 to 64 years, immigrants had lower insurance coverage, health care use, and medical expenditures than US-born adults. Coverage was higher in later eras, but coverage gains and expenditure growth were smaller among immigrants with low income, suggesting that insurance expansion alone may be insufficient to address nativity-related differences in health care access and spending.

item.title: Trends in Direct Oral Anticoagulant Use for Cancer-Associated Venous Thromboembolism
item.dc:creator: Romain Varnier
François Bettega
Aurélie Moskal
Sabine Mainbourg
Mylène Wespiser
Adrien Rousseau
Marie Viprey
item.description:
Authors: Romain Varnier, François Bettega, Aurélie Moskal, Sabine Mainbourg, Mylène Wespiser, Adrien Rousseau, Marie Viprey
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640377
Abstract: Importance Direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) are recommended for selected patients with cancer-associated venous thromboembolism, but their implementation remains heterogeneous. Objective To describe temporal trends in DOAC initiation for cancer-associated venous thromboembolism in France and to identify factors associated with their use. Design, Setting, and Participants This nationwide population-based cohort study included adults without recorded contraindications to DOACs and a first treated venous thromboembolism episode between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2022. Data were collected from the French National Health Data System, a nationwide claims database covering approximately 99% of the population. Analysis was performed from January to August 2025. Exposures Patients were classified into active cancer and no active cancer groups. Covariates included calendar period, patient characteristics, cancer type and treatment, venous thromboembolism characteristics, and initial prescriber setting. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was DOAC initiation within 30 days after the index venous thromboembolism event. Bayesian structural time series models assessed temporal changes across 2016 to 2018, 2019 to 2020, and 2021 to 2022. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with DOAC initiation among patients with active cancer. Results Among 683 184 patients with incident treated venous thromboembolism (median [IQR] age, 67 [53-77] years; 347 421 female [51.0%]), 91 954 patients (13.5%) had active cancer while 591 230 (86.5%) had VTE not associated with active cancer. DOAC use increased from 15.3% (95% CI, 15.0%-15.7%) in 2016 to 2018 to 32.6% (95% CI, 32.1%-33.2%) in 2021 to 2022 among patients with active cancer, and from 63.5% (95% CI, 63.3%-63.7%) to 81.1% (95% CI, 80.9%-81.2%) among patients without active cancer. DOAC initiation increased beyond expected secular trends in patients with active cancer, with relative increases of 20.5% (95% credible interval, 13.0%-27.8%) in 2019 to 2020 and 41.3% (95% credible interval, 32.9%-50.2%) in 2021 to 2022. DOAC initiation was less frequent among patients with comorbidities, history of bleeding, gastrointestinal or gynecologic cancer, active brain metastases, or systemic treatment, and when the initial prescriber was a hospital-based physician rather than a general practitioner. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of patients with incident venous thromboembolism, DOAC use increased substantially in patients with active cancer but remained lower than in patients without active cancer and varied across clinical and care-setting characteristics. This lower uptake may reflect both delayed implementation of recent evidence and the need to individualize anticoagulant selection in complex situations.

item.title: Clinical Walking Speed, Free-Living Walking Cadence, and All-Cause Mortality
item.dc:creator: Rayane Haddadj
Ian Meneghel Danilevicz
Alex V. Rowlands
Vincent T. van Hees
Benjamin Landré
Alexis Le Faucheur
Archana Singh-Manoux

item.description:
Authors: Rayane Haddadj, Ian Meneghel Danilevicz, Alex V. Rowlands, Vincent T. van Hees, Benjamin Landré, Alexis Le Faucheur, Archana Singh-Manoux, Paul Jarle Mork, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640122
Abstract: Importance Walking speed has been shown to be associated with mortality and is conventionally obtained from short walking tests in clinical settings. Free-living walking parameters such as walking cadence can be derived from accelerometers. Objective To examine whether walking parameters measured in clinical and free-living settings are associated with comparable discriminative ability for all-cause mortality risk. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based cohort study, the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the UK, included a baseline from January 2012 to December 2013 and follow-up through August 19, 2024. The study included participants with valid accelerometer data, clinical walking speed, covariates, and electronic health records information. Analyses were performed between September 2025 and February 2026. Exposures Clinical walking speed in meters per second was obtained from a 2.44-m walking test, and 2 free-living metrics of walking cadence in steps per minute (the median walking cadence and the 95th percentile walking cadence) were derived from 9 days of wrist-worn accelerometer data. Main Outcomes and Measures All-cause mortality was ascertained from a British national mortality register. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for all-cause mortality. Discriminative ability was assessed using the Harrel concordance index (C index). Results A total of 4067 participants (mean [SD] age, 69.3 [5.7] years; 3024 males [74.4%]) were included in the analysis. The median (IQR) follow-up was 11.8 (11.5-12.1) years. In models containing mortality risk factors (sociodemographic, behavioral, and health-related factors), higher clinical walking speed (HR, 0.77 [95% CI, 0.71-0.84]), median walking cadence (HR, 0.83 [95% CI, 0.77-0.90]), and 95th percentile walking cadence (HR, 0.82 [95% CI, 0.75-0.89]) were associated with lower all-cause mortality risk (per 1 higher SD) and with a similar discriminative ability (clinical walking speed: C index, 0.747 [95% CI, 0.730-0.764]; median walking cadence: C index, 0.744 [95% CI, 0.726-0.761]; and 95th percentile walking cadence: C index, 0.745 [95% CI, 0.727-0.762]). Only clinical walking speed was associated with an improved discriminative ability of a model including mortality risk factors. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence were both associated with all-cause mortality risk and had a similar discriminative ability for all-cause mortality. These results suggest that both measures can be used in population-based studies, and the choice between the 2 methods may depend on research objectives, implementation constraints, and the strengths of each method.
